lesson.title: Adding Up the Arrows: Molecular Dipole Moment
lesson.summary: A molecule's overall polarity depends not just on whether it contains polar bonds but on how those bond dipoles are arranged in three dimensional space, since a symmetric geometry can cancel them out entirely.
lesson.body:
A molecular dipole moment is the vector sum of every individual bond dipole in a molecule, meaning you have to add up not just how strong each bond dipole is but also which direction it points. Dipole moments are measured in a unit called the debye, abbreviated D. This vector nature is the single most important idea in this concept, because it means a molecule can be built entirely out of polar bonds and still end up with zero net dipole moment overall, if its geometry happens to point those individual bond dipoles in directions that cancel.

This is exactly why molecular geometry, not just bond polarity, has to enter the picture. Two molecules can have chemically identical types of polar bonds and still differ completely in overall polarity, purely because one is symmetric enough to cancel its bond dipoles and the other is not. Predicting a molecule's polarity correctly always requires two separate steps: first identify whether its bonds are polar using electronegativity difference, and second, use the molecular shape from VSEPR to work out whether those bond dipoles reinforce or cancel each other.

Carbon dioxide shows cancellation clearly. Each C=O bond is meaningfully polar, since oxygen and carbon have a delta EN of about 0.89. But CO2's carbon is sp hybridized with two electron domains and no lone pairs, giving the molecule a perfectly linear, 180 degree shape. The two C=O bond dipoles point in exactly opposite directions along that straight line, and being equal in strength, they cancel each other completely. The net dipole moment of CO2 is zero, making it a nonpolar molecule despite being built entirely from polar bonds.

Water shows the opposite outcome. Each O-H bond is polar, with a delta EN of about 1.24, comparable in strength to the C=O bonds in CO2. But water's oxygen carries two lone pairs, and as established with lone pair repulsion, this bends the molecule to a measured angle of about 104.5 degrees rather than the 180 degrees seen in CO2. At that bent angle, the two O-H bond dipoles do not point in opposite directions, so they do not cancel, and they add together into a substantial net dipole moment, commonly cited at about 1.85 D. This is a major reason water is such an effective solvent for other polar substances and ions.

Carbon tetrachloride, CCl4, offers one more clean contrast. Its four C-Cl bonds are individually polar, but its sp3 hybridized carbon has no lone pairs and a perfectly symmetric tetrahedral shape, so the four bond dipoles cancel completely by symmetry, exactly as in CO2, giving CCl4 a net dipole moment of zero. Replace just one of those four chlorine atoms with a hydrogen, forming chloroform, CHCl3, and that symmetry breaks: the bond dipoles no longer point in a pattern that cancels, and the molecule becomes measurably polar. The lesson across all of these examples is the same one: whether a molecule is polar depends on polar bonds and molecular geometry acting together, never on either one alone.
